paras: The March 1903 Bungaloo attacks in Indianapolis were pursuits of Black men through downtown Indianapolis, Indiana, on the night of Sunday, March 8, 1903, by white youths known as the "Bungaloos." The crowd, which grew to nearly five hundred, chased at least five men with cries of "Kill the niggers!"; all escaped, and no injuries or arrests were reported. The Indianapolis Freeman wrote that the city had "narrowly escaped a lynching scene."

According to the Indianapolis Journal, the trouble began about 8 p.m. near the New Claypool Hotel, when two Black men, said to be drunk, passed the corner "cursing and abusing" white men and women. Bungaloo members joined the crowd that gathered and, to cries of "Kill the niggers!", chased the pair until they boarded a street car on Illinois Street.

The crowd then turned on "any negro that happened to pass." Bluford Williams, a Sentinel employee, fled into the Sentinel building and came back with a revolver to find his pursuers gone, and George Kinslow, described as "a mulatto," was chased half a block before catching a street car. At 11 p.m. another man escaped the crowd near the post office by running into an office building. The attackers threw missiles, and the Journal said the "ruffians ran wild" despite the police on duty downtown.
No report of arrests, injuries or an official inquiry appears in the coverage.

The Journal ran its local report the next morning under the headline "Bungaloos on Warpath," with a subhead blaming "Two Intoxicated Colored Men." It mocked boys "thirsting for the blood of some Ethiopian" and faulted the police, but named neither of the first two men.

Six days later the Freeman, a Black weekly, repeated as hearsay that "two drunken Negroes caused the row" and condemned both the men and the Bungaloos. It warned that men who defied race feeling did so "at their peril," yet insisted that "the police and not the mob" should have acted.

reader.title: March 1903 Bungaloo attacks in Indianapolis
bases: A crowd of white youths, the Bungaloos, chased several Black men through downtown streets with cries to kill them and threw missiles, but caught and injured no one (A1); the Freeman called it a narrowly escaped lynching scene (A2).

No one was killed: every man pursued escaped (A1). The crowd of up to five hundred acted without authority on a story that two Black men had insulted whites, and then against any Black passerby (A1, A2), so it was at most a threatened or attempted lynching.

The only detailed report is the Indianapolis Journal's (A1); the Freeman's editorial confirms that the melee happened but relies on 'the reports' and 'it is said' (A2), so it is not an independent account.

accounts.label: Local white daily
accounts.gist: The Bungaloos, joined by a crowd of up to five hundred, hunted Black men downtown for three hours after two drunken Black men cursed whites; police on duty did not stop them.

accounts.label: Black weekly editorial
accounts.gist: From the reports, two drunken Negroes caused the row; the city narrowly escaped a lynching, and the police rather than the Bungaloos should have dealt with the men.

framing.detail: Headline 'Bungaloos on Warpath' with subhead blaming 'Two Intoxicated Colored Men'; calls the attackers 'ruffians' and mocks their thirst 'for the blood of some Ethiopian' while faulting police inaction.
Condemns the Bungaloos and says a lynching would have added 'further disgrace', but also condemns the 'rowdy' men and warns that defying race feeling is done 'at their peril'.

info: Night of Sunday, 1903-03-08, about 8 to 11 p.m.
Downtown Indianapolis: New Claypool Hotel corner, Illinois, Washington, Meridian and Pennsylvania streets, the Sentinel building, near the post office
Two unnamed Black men (first pursued); Bluford Williams, a Sentinel employee known as 'Black Annie'; George Kinslow, 'a mulatto'; an unnamed Black man near the post office
The two men first pursued were said to have passed the corner drunk, cursing and abusing white men and women; the others were accused of nothing
The 'Bungaloos', young white boys and rowdies led by a 'chief', with a larger crowd of onlookers

sources.note: Local next-morning report 'Bungaloos on Warpath': three hours of pursuits, names Bluford Williams and George Kinslow, crowd of nearly 500, police did not stop it.
quotes: For three hours last night the Bungaloos had control of the down-town streets and caused terror to many negroes that happened along.
Despite the number of police on duty on the down-town streets, ruffians ran wild, yelling, shouting and throwing missiles after fleeing negroes.
The Bungaloos, failing to capture their prey, turned their attention next to any negro that happened to pass.
